Chapter 37

Streamed loads: await what paints, stream what waits

The rule for deciding, and the .catch that is not defensive programming.

By the end of this chapter

Send HTML immediately and let the slow half arrive later, without breaking hydration.

Two returned values, and the difference between them is the whole lesson. q and range come straight off the URL and the page cannot render without them — there is no sensible loading state for the contents of a query box, and rendering an empty one that fills in a moment later means the editor is briefly wrong and the caret jumps.

services is a promise, returned unawaited. SvelteKit streams it: the HTML goes out immediately and the value arrives in a later chunk. It feeds completion, which nobody can use until they have focused the editor and typed something.

The .catch is load-bearing, not defensive

A rejection in a streamed promise arrives after the response has started, so it cannot become an error page. It becomes an unhandled rejection in the browser and a page that never finishes hydrating — a blank interface with no error anywhere. Resolving to an empty list degrades completion and nothing else.

Reading it without waiting for it

The editor is drawn at once, on the server as well, and its catalogue reads services.current: an empty list in the first paint, and the streamed list as soon as it lands. Nothing on the screen depends on it except the completion list, and nobody asks for a completion in the first moment of a page. When the list arrives, the editor is not drawn again — the same textarea, with the same caret, simply has more to offer.

A stand-in until the promise resolves, then the value, in a $state.raw field. Raw, because the value is replaced whole and never changed in place, so a deep proxy around it would be work for nothing. The page creates one inside a $derived, so a navigation that streams a new list makes a new Streamed, and the old one is dropped with the promise it was waiting for.

Why not {#await data.services then services}

That was the first version, and it cost two things. “During server-side rendering, only the pending branch will be rendered”, and the pending branch here was empty, so the editor was the one control missing from the server’s HTML: a link to a refused query, opened before the JavaScript arrived, explained the refusal and offered nowhere to fix it. And in the browser the then branch is drawn from scratch when the promise lands, so an editor inside it is a new editor — an early click or a caret placed while the list was in flight would be thrown away. The block is the right tool when the content *is* the value; here the value only improves a control that is useful without it.

Not an $effect that copies the value into $state either. An effect would need a flag to ignore a promise that landed after it had been replaced, and an effect that writes state another rune could hold is the pattern the $effect documentation warns against. A small class keeps the promise and the state it settles into together, and the $derived that creates it decides when it is replaced.

The rule, stated once

Await what the first paint needs; stream what the first interaction needs. Streaming everything is a page of spinners. Awaiting everything is a page that waits for its slowest query.

Checkpoint

  • The explore page, editor and rows, is in the server’s HTML before the completion catalogue has loaded.
  • Completion still offers service names once the catalogue lands, and the caret does not move when it does.
  • A failing catalogue query degrades completion and nothing else.
  • You can say which of your loads should be awaited and why.
